options.a: Stratum basale (germinativum)
options.b: Stratum spinosum (prickle layer)
options.c: Stratum granulosum (granular layer)
options.d: Stratum lucidum (clear layer)

distractorExplanations.b: The spinosum holds keratinocytes and Langerhans cells and receives melanin granules, but melanocytes sit in the basal layer.
distractorExplanations.c: The granulosum is where keratinocytes fill with keratohyalin and begin to die; melanocytes are in the stratum basale.
distractorExplanations.d: The lucidum is a thin clear layer found only in thick skin of the palms and soles; it does not house melanocytes.

options.a: Sweat that helps regulate body temperature
options.b: Sebum (oil) that helps lubricate skin and hair
options.c: Keratin that strengthens the outer skin layer
options.d: Apocrine secretions that cause body odor

distractorExplanations.a: Sweat for temperature regulation comes from sudoriferous (eccrine) glands, not sebaceous glands.
distractorExplanations.c: Keratin is produced by keratinocytes in the epidermis; sebaceous glands secrete sebum into the follicle.
distractorExplanations.d: Apocrine glands in the underarm and groin produce secretions that bacteria break down into odor; sebaceous glands make oil.

options.a: A contagious bacterial infection of the face similar to impetigo
options.b: A chronic inflammatory condition with flushing, visible vessels
options.c: A form of acne vulgaris caused by blocked comedones and treated by extraction
options.d: A temporary allergic reaction that clears once the irritating product is stopped

distractorExplanations.a: Rosacea is not contagious or bacterial like impetigo; it is a chronic inflammatory vascular condition.
distractorExplanations.c: Rosacea lacks comedones and is not acne vulgaris; extraction can worsen the inflammation and redness.
distractorExplanations.d: Product triggers can flare rosacea, but the condition is chronic and does not resolve when a product is stopped.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-skin-s.explanation: Rosacea is chronic/inflammatory; triggers and medical care matter; it is not managed like simple comedones only. Papules and pustules may also occur, and extraction alone does not cure it.

options.a: Melanin production / melanocyte activity
options.b: Keratinocyte turnover in the stratum corneum
options.c: Hemoglobin and blood flow in dermal capillaries
options.d: Carotene stored in the subcutaneous fat layer

distractorExplanations.b: Faster or slower cell turnover affects texture and dullness; sun-induced darkening comes from increased melanin production.
distractorExplanations.c: Increased blood flow causes redness (erythema), such as sunburn; the lasting brown color is from melanin.
distractorExplanations.d: Carotene gives a yellowish tint from diet and is not stimulated by UV; tanning and sun spots are melanin.

options.a: Closed comedones and mild congestion across the forehead and chin
options.b: Active herpes simplex lesion (cold sore) in the treatment area
options.c: Dehydrated skin with fine lines around the eyes
options.d: Healed acne scarring from several years earlier

distractorExplanations.a: Closed comedones are a common indication for exfoliation and extractions, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.c: Dehydration calls for gentler products and hydration, but it does not require clearance before service.
distractorExplanations.d: Old, healed scars are intact skin and are often treated with exfoliation; active lesions are the concern.

options.a: An acquired loss of pigment in patches caused by autoimmune melanocyte damage
options.b: A localized patch of excess melanin from sun exposure
options.c: A genetic lack of melanin production leading to very light skin/hair
options.d: Reduced pigment after injury or inflammation that may slowly return

distractorExplanations.a: Acquired patchy depigmentation from autoimmune melanocyte loss describes vitiligo, not genetic albinism.
distractorExplanations.b: A localized sun-induced patch of extra melanin is a lentigo or hyperpigmentation, the opposite of albinism.
distractorExplanations.d: Pigment loss after injury or inflammation is post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, which is acquired and local.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-skin-s.explanation: Albinism is a melanin synthesis disorder; sun protection education is critical. Light sensitivity is a major concern, so sun protection education is essential.

options.a: Secretion, through sebaceous gland output of sebum
options.b: Excretion, through sweat glands releasing salts and waste
options.c: Sensation, through nerve endings in the dermis that detect heat, cold, and touch
options.d: Absorption / metabolic functions of skin (vitamin D production pathway)

distractorExplanations.a: Secretion refers to sebum output that lubricates the skin; it is not the vitamin D pathway.
distractorExplanations.b: Excretion covers sweat removing salts and waste; vitamin D synthesis is not a sweat-gland function.
distractorExplanations.c: Sensation describes nerve endings responding to touch, heat, and pain; it plays no role in vitamin D production.

options.a: Genetic predisposition inherited from the client's parents
options.b: Chronic unprotected UV exposure (photoaging)
options.c: Natural decline of collagen with chronological age
options.d: Hormonal changes during menopause

distractorExplanations.a: Genetics drive intrinsic aging; the prompt asks about extrinsic (environmental) factors, led by UV exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: Gradual collagen loss with age is intrinsic aging; extrinsic aging is driven mainly by sun exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: Menopausal hormone shifts are an intrinsic aging factor; UV exposure is the leading extrinsic factor.

options.a: A fungal infection of the scalp seen mostly in children
options.b: A yeast overgrowth causing light patches on the trunk
options.c: A fungal (ringworm) infection of the body skin
options.d: A viral infection causing raised flesh-colored warts

distractorExplanations.a: Fungal infection of the scalp is tinea capitis; tinea corporis affects the skin of the body.
distractorExplanations.b: Light or dark patches on the trunk from Malassezia yeast describe tinea versicolor, not ringworm of the body.
distractorExplanations.d: Raised warts are verrucae caused by HPV, a virus; tinea corporis is a dermatophyte fungal infection.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-skin-s.explanation: Tinea is dermatophyte infection; estheticians should recognize and not treat as cosmetic acne. Refer the client and avoid services that could spread it.

options.a: Remove makeup, oil, and debris to prepare skin for treatment
options.b: Exfoliate dead surface cells so later products can penetrate deeper
options.c: Restore the skin's pH after the cleanser is applied
options.d: Soften sebum in follicles to prepare for extractions

distractorExplanations.b: Removing dead cells is the exfoliation step, which follows cleansing; cleansing removes makeup, oil, and debris.
distractorExplanations.c: Rebalancing pH after cleansing is the purpose of toner, not the cleansing step itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Softening sebum before extractions is the role of steam or desincrustation, which come after cleansing.

options.a: Treat acne bacteria with blue-light photomodulation
options.b: Magnify the skin with a cool light for close inspection
options.c: Analyze pigmentation, oiliness, and certain skin conditions
options.d: Warm the skin with infrared heat before extractions

distractorExplanations.a: Blue-light acne treatment is done with LED devices; a Wood's lamp is a diagnostic UV viewing tool.
distractorExplanations.b: Magnification under cool white light is the magnifying lamp (loupe); a Wood's lamp uses filtered UV light.
distractorExplanations.d: Infrared lamps provide heat; a Wood's lamp emits UV light for analysis and does not warm the skin.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Wood’s lamp helps visualization; it is not a treatment device for cutting or permanent hair removal alone. It works by viewing the skin under UV illumination.

options.a: Push water-soluble products into skin through polarity
options.b: Emulsify sebum before extractions using negative polarity
options.c: Tone facial muscles with rhythmic contractions
options.d: Create a germicidal / stimulating effect

distractorExplanations.a: Introducing water-soluble products by polarity is galvanic iontophoresis, not high-frequency current.
distractorExplanations.b: Saponifying sebum with the negative pole is galvanic desincrustation; high frequency is an alternating current.
distractorExplanations.c: Muscle contraction is produced by microcurrent or faradic/sinusoidal current, not by Tesla high frequency.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: HF is a modality for suitable clients; it is not diagnosis or ablative laser. It uses oxygenating sparking on suitable skin.

options.a: Working only on appropriate lesions with hygiene, gentle technique
options.b: Extracting pustules and papules with firm pressure in one session
options.c: Using fingertips wrapped in dry cotton on unsteamed, unsoftened skin
options.d: Extracting before cleansing, so pores are not closed by products

distractorExplanations.b: Papules are inflamed and not extractable, and firm pressure risks scarring and spreading infection.
distractorExplanations.c: Skin should be softened first and gloved fingers with damp cotton used; dry cotton on unsoftened skin tears tissue.
distractorExplanations.d: Skin is cleansed and softened before extractions; extracting through makeup and debris drives bacteria into the follicle.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Safe extractions require judgment, sanitation, and limits; cysts/herpes need medical care. The esthetician must also know the contraindications.

options.a: Dry/dehydrated skin to add moisture and soften lines
options.b: Oily/congested skin to absorb excess sebum
options.c: Sensitive/couperose skin to calm redness and heat
options.d: Mature skin to firm by forming an occlusive film

distractorExplanations.a: Clay absorbs oil and can dry the skin further; dry or dehydrated skin calls for cream or hydrating masks.
distractorExplanations.c: Clay can be drying and stimulating; sensitive or couperose skin usually gets soothing gel or cream masks.
distractorExplanations.d: Forming an occlusive film describes paraffin or modelling masks, not clay, which absorbs oil.

options.a: Pushing an acidic, positively charged product into the skin using the positive pole
options.b: Tightening pores with the positive pole after extractions
options.c: Softening sebum/debris (anaphoresis) to aid cleansing of congested skin
options.d: Producing a germicidal spark that dries pustules on contact

distractorExplanations.a: Introducing acidic products with the positive pole is cataphoresis/iontophoresis, not desincrustation.
distractorExplanations.b: The positive pole's astringent effect is used after treatment; desincrustation uses the negative pole to soften sebum.
distractorExplanations.d: A germicidal spark comes from high-frequency current, not from galvanic desincrustation.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Desincrustation uses galvanic polarity effects; it is not cryo, tattooing, or cutting. It is used only when appropriate for the client.

options.a: Dehydrated skin that needs moisture rather than oil control
options.b: Pregnancy (for certain modalities) / metal implants / pacemakers
options.c: Recent use of a daily SPF moisturizer on the treatment area
options.d: Congested skin with closed comedones on the chin and forehead

distractorExplanations.a: Dehydration is a skin condition to address with product choice, not a medical contraindication to heat devices.
distractorExplanations.c: Daily sunscreen is routine protective care and is removed during cleansing; it does not contraindicate machines.
distractorExplanations.d: Congestion is a common indication for steam and other facial machines, not a reason to avoid them.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Electromagnetic/heat modalities have medical contraindications; always screen. Contraindications depend on the device, so follow the manufacturer and the law.

options.a: Exfoliation → cleanse → client consultation
options.b: Toner → cleanse → consultation once makeup is removed
options.c: Client consultation/skin analysis → cleanse
options.d: Mask → makeup removal → consultation

distractorExplanations.a: Exfoliating before consultation skips contraindication screening, and exfoliation follows cleansing.
distractorExplanations.b: Toner follows cleansing, and consultation comes first so contraindications are known before any product touches skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Masks come near the end of a facial, after cleansing and treatment; consultation always comes first.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Consultation and cleansing set safety and efficacy for subsequent steps. Then continue with exfoliation and treatment steps as planned.

options.a: Thermal resurfacing that removes the epidermis
options.b: Permanent hair reduction by targeting melanin
options.c: UV exposure to stimulate a cosmetic tan
options.d: Non-thermal photomodulation benefits

distractorExplanations.a: Removing the epidermis with heat is ablative laser resurfacing, a medical procedure; LED is non-thermal.
distractorExplanations.b: Targeting follicle melanin for hair reduction is laser or IPL; LED does not destroy hair follicles.
distractorExplanations.c: Esthetic LEDs emit visible or near-infrared light, not tanning UV, and do not stimulate a tan.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: LED is adjunctive; it is not surgery, sunscreen, or prescription medicine. Examples include calming or acne-support protocols, depending on wavelength.

options.a: Toward lymphatic drainage patterns with appropriate pressure
options.b: Deep petrissage over the eyelids to stimulate circulation
options.c: Brisk tapotement over active acne lesions to stimulate faster healing
options.d: Firm movements from muscle origin toward insertion

distractorExplanations.b: The delicate eye area gets only light effleurage; deep kneading over the eyelids is contraindicated.
distractorExplanations.c: Stimulating movements over active inflamed acne spread bacteria and worsen inflammation; avoid those areas.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the standard direction: facial massage moves from the insertion toward the origin of the muscle.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Esthetic massage is gentle and purposeful; avoid contraindicated areas and poor hygiene. Adjust to the client's skin and contraindications.

options.a: Lower pH means a gentler peel at the same acid percentage
options.b: Deeper/higher-strength peels increase results and risks
options.c: Peel percentage alone sets strength, apart from pH and formulation
options.d: Glycolic and TCA peels penetrate to the same depth at equal strength

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the relationship: a lower pH leaves more free acid, making the peel stronger, not gentler.
distractorExplanations.c: Strength depends on pH, pKa, vehicle, and layers as well as percentage; percentage alone does not define it.
distractorExplanations.d: Different acids behave differently; TCA coagulates proteins and penetrates deeper than glycolic at comparable percentages.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Acid type, pH, vehicle, and layers matter; professional judgment and scope are essential. Stay within license, training, and manufacturer protocols.

options.a: Absorb excess oil and tighten pores on oily, congested skin
options.b: Calm active rosacea flares with gentle, sustained warmth
options.c: Provide emollient occlusion and comfort, often for dry skin
options.d: Exfoliate dead cells as the wax hardens and is peeled away

distractorExplanations.a: Absorbing oil from congested skin is the role of clay masks; paraffin is occlusive and suited to dry skin.
distractorExplanations.b: Heat is a common rosacea trigger, so warm paraffin is avoided on flaring or vascular skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Paraffin is used for warmth and occlusion; exfoliation is done with enzymes, acids, or mechanical methods.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-treatm.explanation: Warm paraffin can hydrate/comfort suitable intact skin; not for infection or medical surgery. It is used on the face or hands when appropriate.

options.a: Sterilization
options.b: High-level disinfection
options.c: Sanitation
options.d: Antisepsis

distractorExplanations.b: High-level disinfection kills most microbes but not large numbers of bacterial spores; only sterilization kills all.
distractorExplanations.c: Sanitation (cleaning) only lowers the number of microbes and removes debris; it is the lowest level of decontamination.
distractorExplanations.d: Antisepsis reduces microbes on living skin and is not a level of tool decontamination that destroys spores.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-infect.explanation: Sterilization kills spores; disinfection reduces pathogens on nonliving surfaces but may not kill all spores. Single-use disposables are the alternative where regulations allow.

options.a: High-level disinfection followed by dry storage
options.b: Sterilization (or single-use disposable) per regulations
options.c: EPA hospital disinfectant with a 10-minute contact time
options.d: Cleaning with soap and water, then UV cabinet storage

distractorExplanations.a: High-level disinfection suits mucous-membrane items; implements that penetrate tissue or contact blood need sterilization.
distractorExplanations.c: Hospital disinfectants are for nonporous noncritical tools; blood-contact implements need sterilization or disposal.
distractorExplanations.d: Soap cleaning is only the first step and UV cabinets are storage, not sterilization of blood-contact implements.

options.a: After each client, with gloves covering hand hygiene before services
options.b: Before each client, using alcohol rub even when hands are visibly soiled
options.c: Before and after each client and whenever hands are contaminated
options.d: At the start and end of each shift and after eating

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; hands are washed before putting on gloves for each client as well as after.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol rub does not remove visible soil; soiled hands need soap and water, and hygiene is needed after services too.
distractorExplanations.d: Shift-based washing skips the before-and-after-each-client moments that prevent cross-contamination.

options.a: At double the label concentration for faster kill
options.b: Wiped on and dried immediately so no residue is left on tools
options.c: Mixed fresh weekly and reused until the solution looks cloudy
options.d: According to label contact time, dilution, and intended surface use

distractorExplanations.a: Using more than the label dilution is off-label, can damage tools and skin, and does not shorten contact time.
distractorExplanations.b: Surfaces must stay wet for the full label contact time; immediate drying prevents the disinfectant from working.
distractorExplanations.c: Most labels and boards require fresh solution daily or when contaminated; clear-looking solution can still be ineffective.

options.a: Cotton rounds / wooden spatulas that cannot be properly disinfected
options.b: Metal comedone extractors that are cleaned and disinfected after each use
options.c: Glass bowls used for mixing masks between clients
options.d: Plastic mask brushes washed with soap and stored dry

distractorExplanations.b: Nonporous metal extractors are multi-use when cleaned and disinfected or sterilized as the state requires.
distractorExplanations.c: Glass is nonporous and can be cleaned and disinfected, so mask bowls are multi-use items.
distractorExplanations.d: Nonporous synthetic brushes can be cleaned and disinfected and are multi-use; porous items like cotton are discarded.

options.a: Apply a styptic pencil to the cut and continue the service
options.b: Stop service, don PPE as needed, clean, apply antiseptic/bandage
options.c: Disinfect the wound with the EPA tool disinfectant, then continue
options.d: Finish the service, then clean the area and record the incident

distractorExplanations.a: Styptic pencils cross-contaminate; use single-use styptic powder or liquid, and stop service to manage the exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: EPA-registered disinfectants are for nonliving surfaces only; wounds get an antiseptic, not a tool disinfectant.
distractorExplanations.d: Service stops immediately after a blood exposure; delaying cleanup spreads contamination to client and implements.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-infect.explanation: Exposure control plans protect client and practitioner. Then disinfect, document, and follow the exposure plan.

options.a: Sterilants that kill bacterial spores on tools
options.b: Antiseptics for cleansing the client's skin before waxing
options.c: Disinfectants for nonporous surfaces/tools
options.d: Disinfectants for porous items like buffers and pumice

distractorExplanations.a: Quats are not sporicidal and do not sterilize; spores require an autoclave or a registered sterilant.
distractorExplanations.b: Antiseptics for skin are formulated for living tissue; quat disinfectants are for nonliving surfaces.
distractorExplanations.d: Porous items cannot be reliably disinfected and are discarded after use; quats are for nonporous items.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-infect.explanation: Many salon disinfectants are quat-based; sterilization is a higher process, often autoclave/chemical sterilant under strict rules. They work when formulated and used per label.

options.a: Herpes simplex (viral)—work around the lesion carefully
options.b: Tinea faciei (fungal)—treat with an antifungal mask
options.c: Perioral dermatitis (inflammatory)—not contagious
options.d: Impetigo (bacterial)—do not perform services; refer

distractorExplanations.a: Herpes forms grouped vesicles rather than honey-colored crusts, and active lesions are a contraindication, not worked around.
distractorExplanations.b: Tinea forms scaly rings, not honey crusts, and estheticians refer rather than treat infections.
distractorExplanations.c: Perioral dermatitis causes small red papules around the mouth, not honey-colored crusts, and is not impetigo.

options.a: Using closed containers for soiled linens
options.b: Storing soiled towels in an open hamper until day's end
options.c: Washing towels in cold water with fabric softener only
options.d: Air-drying lightly used towels for reuse on the next client

distractorExplanations.b: Soiled linens must go in a covered container to keep contaminants out of the treatment area air and surfaces.
distractorExplanations.c: Boards require washing with detergent (and often hot water or bleach) per rules; softener does not sanitize.
distractorExplanations.d: Every towel is single-client; once used it must be laundered before reuse, however lightly used.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-infect.explanation: Linens can harbor microbes; control contamination and wash properly. Wash with appropriate detergent and hot water per state rules.

options.a: Protect workers from hazardous chemicals through SDS and labeling
options.b: Protect workers from occupational exposure to blood and OPIM
options.c: Protect clients from infection through state board sanitation rules
options.d: Require EPA registration of salon disinfectants

distractorExplanations.a: Chemical hazard information through SDS and labels is OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, a different rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Client sanitation rules come from the state board; the BBP Standard protects employees from occupational exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: Disinfectant registration is handled by the EPA under FIFRA, not by OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.

options.a: Reuse one spatula throughout the service, dipping back into the jar
options.b: Apply product with gloved fingers from the jar after cleansing
options.c: Dispense with clean spatulas/pumps; do not double-dip fingers into jars
options.d: Return unused product from the bowl to the jar to avoid waste

distractorExplanations.a: Dipping a spatula that has touched the client back into the jar contaminates the product; use a clean spatula each time.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloved fingers that touched the client still contaminate the jar; dispense with a clean spatula or pump instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Dispensed product is considered contaminated and must be discarded, never returned to the original container.

options.a: Dry heat at high temperature for an extended cycle
options.b: Ultraviolet light inside a closed cabinet
options.c: Chemical immersion in a high-level disinfectant
options.d: Steam under pressure (moist heat)

distractorExplanations.a: Dry heat sterilizers are a separate device; an autoclave uses pressurized steam, which sterilizes faster.
distractorExplanations.b: UV cabinets are for storage and do not sterilize; autoclaves use steam under pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Chemical immersion is a disinfection method; an autoclave sterilizes with moist heat under pressure.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-infect.explanation: Steam autoclaves are a standard sterilization method when used/validated correctly. The cycle must reach validated time, temperature, and pressure.

options.a: Keep items wet with disinfectant for the full 10 minutes
options.b: Spray once, then wipe dry as soon as surfaces look clean
options.c: Immerse items for 10 minutes only if blood was present
options.d: Let the solution air-dry, even if it evaporates before the time

distractorExplanations.b: Looking clean is not the endpoint; the surface must remain wet for the full labeled contact time.
distractorExplanations.c: The label contact time applies to every disinfection, not only after blood exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: If the disinfectant dries before the contact time ends, the kill claim is not met; reapply to keep it wet.

options.a: Bacteria, including those that cause staph infections
options.b: Fungi, including those that cause tinea infections
options.c: Viruses (as stated on the label for listed organisms)
options.d: Bacterial spores, as required for sterilization

distractorExplanations.a: Effectiveness against bacteria such as staph is a bactericidal claim, not a virucidal one.
distractorExplanations.b: Effectiveness against fungi such as tinea is a fungicidal claim, separate from a virucidal claim.
distractorExplanations.d: Killing spores is a sporicidal (sterilant) claim; virucidal means effective against the listed viruses.

options.a: The scope defined by state law/regulations and their license
options.b: Any service covered by their manufacturer device training
options.c: The services their employer's medical director approves
options.d: The national scope set by the NIC for all states

distractorExplanations.b: Manufacturer training does not expand legal scope; the state license and regulations define what is permitted.
distractorExplanations.c: A medical director cannot authorize services outside the esthetician's state-defined scope of practice.
distractorExplanations.d: NIC develops licensing exams; each state's law and board rules set the esthetician's scope.

options.a: Having the client sign an intake form listing medications, without discussion
options.b: Explaining the service, risks/benefits/alternatives, and obtaining client agreement
options.c: Explaining risks after the service if the client has a reaction
options.d: Obtaining a signature once per year that covers any service offered

distractorExplanations.a: An intake form screens health history; informed consent also requires explaining the service, risks, and alternatives.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent must be informed before treatment; explaining risks afterward cannot make the service consented.
distractorExplanations.d: Consent is service-specific; a blanket annual signature does not inform the client about a particular treatment's risks.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-laws-b.explanation: Consent is a process plus documentation—not silence. Consent is obtained before proceeding.

options.a: Shared with product vendors to tailor client recommendations
options.b: Kept until the client's next visit, then discarded
options.c: Accurate, confidential, and retained according to law/policy
options.d: Updated by removing outdated reactions to keep files current

distractorExplanations.a: Client records are confidential and cannot be shared with vendors without the client's authorization.
distractorExplanations.b: Records are kept for the period required by state law or policy, not discarded after the next appointment.
distractorExplanations.d: Past adverse reactions must stay in the record; deleting them is falsification and hides important history.

options.a: Perform a gentler extraction since the client is already in the chair
options.b: Respect the refusal but leave it out of the record to avoid liability
options.c: Stop the service at that point and charge for the full facial
options.d: Respect the refusal, document, and adapt the service appropriately

distractorExplanations.a: Any extraction after a refusal is unconsented touching, however gentle; the client's decision must be respected.
distractorExplanations.b: A refusal should be documented; omitting it weakens the record and the practitioner's legal protection.
distractorExplanations.c: The service can be adapted rather than ended, and charging for undelivered work is unethical billing.

options.a: False/misleading advertising and practicing beyond scope
options.b: Acceptable if the menu adds 'Botox-like' in small print
options.c: Permitted if the topical cream contains peptides
options.d: A trademark matter only, not a licensing issue

distractorExplanations.b: Fine print does not cure a misleading service name; implying injectables without authorization is still deceptive.
distractorExplanations.c: Peptide ingredients do not make a topical product Botox; using the trademark misleads clients about the service.
distractorExplanations.d: Beyond trademark concerns, boards treat false advertising and implied out-of-scope services as license violations.

options.a: Expand the license to include injections after enough hours
options.b: Maintain competency and meet license renewal standards
options.c: Replace the need to follow updated state sanitation rules
options.d: Certify estheticians to work in any state without reciprocity

distractorExplanations.a: Continuing education does not expand scope; injections remain medical procedures requiring medical licensure.
distractorExplanations.c: CE often teaches updated rules but never substitutes for following current state infection-control regulations.
distractorExplanations.d: CE hours keep a license current in its state; working elsewhere requires that state's licensure or reciprocity.

options.a: Follow employer policy, since the employer holds the salon license
options.b: Follow whichever rule the client prefers for their service
options.c: Follow the stricter/legal requirement
options.d: Follow the law in services, but employer policy in sanitation

distractorExplanations.a: An establishment license does not let the employer override state law; the practitioner's license is also at stake.
distractorExplanations.b: Client preference cannot override legal requirements or employer safety policies.
distractorExplanations.d: State sanitation rules are law too; an employer policy cannot set a lower sanitation standard.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-laws-b.explanation: Law controls practice; policies cannot authorize illegal acts. An employer policy can never authorize violating the law.

options.a: License discipline, civil liability, and harm to clients
options.b: A warning only, since boards do not discipline for health issues
options.c: Liability for the salon owner, with the esthetician protected
options.d: Consequences limited to a fine paid by the employer

distractorExplanations.b: Boards can suspend or revoke licenses for unsafe practice, including working while contagious.
distractorExplanations.c: The practitioner who performs the service is personally liable and subject to discipline, not just the owner.
distractorExplanations.d: Consequences can include license discipline, civil suits, and client harm, not just an employer fine.

options.a: Recommending products by commission level rather than skin need
options.b: Clean attire, hygiene, respectful communication, and sober practice
options.c: Discussing other clients' results by name to build trust
options.d: Wearing open-toed shoes and loose jewelry for comfort

distractorExplanations.a: Commission-driven recommendations put sales ahead of client welfare, which is unprofessional conduct.
distractorExplanations.c: Naming other clients breaches confidentiality, even when the intent is to build credibility.
distractorExplanations.d: Open-toed shoes and dangling jewelry create safety and hygiene risks; professional dress is clean and practical.

options.a: Confirm skin type by observing oil on a blotting tissue
options.b: Determine peel depth by measuring frosting on the forearm
options.c: Screen for adverse reactions on a small area before full application
options.d: Desensitize the skin so that a later allergic reaction becomes less likely

distractorExplanations.a: Blotting tissue helps assess oiliness during skin analysis; a patch test checks for reactions to a product.
distractorExplanations.b: Frosting is an endpoint observed during some peels, not the purpose of a patch test.
distractorExplanations.d: A patch test screens for sensitivity; it does not build tolerance or prevent future reactions.

options.a: Relying on the manufacturer's statement that the device is FDA-cleared
options.b: Following what other spas in the area offer on their menus
options.c: Completing the device company's certification course
options.d: Checking state board rules and whether medical oversight is required

distractorExplanations.a: FDA clearance concerns device safety, not who may operate it; scope is set by state law and the board.
distractorExplanations.b: Competitors may be operating outside scope; their menus are not a legal authority.
distractorExplanations.c: A manufacturer certificate shows training but does not grant legal authority to perform the service.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-laws-b.explanation: Regulation varies; verify before offering. Manufacturer training is also checked before offering the service.

options.a: Health history, photos, and treatment notes from unauthorized disclosure
options.b: Health history only, with before/after photos free to post
options.c: Treatment notes, while the client's name may be freely shared on social media
options.d: Records while the client is active, ending once they stop visiting

distractorExplanations.b: Client photos are protected too; posting them requires the client's written consent.
distractorExplanations.c: A client's identity is confidential; naming clients publicly without consent breaches privacy.
distractorExplanations.d: The duty of confidentiality continues after the client stops visiting.

options.a: Acceptable if the product was opened
options.b: Fraudulent/unethical billing
options.c: A permitted package-pricing practice
options.d: Legal if disclosed after the visit

distractorExplanations.a: Opening a product does not justify billing for a service that was never performed.
distractorExplanations.c: Package pricing bundles services the client receives; charging for undelivered services is billing fraud.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure after the fact does not make billing for an unperformed service legal or ethical.

options.a: Treat it with a gentle facial while the client waits for an appointment
options.b: Recommend an over-the-counter product and recheck in two weeks
options.c: Refer to a licensed physician/dermatologist
options.d: Proceed with the service if the client signs a waiver

distractorExplanations.a: Treating a medical skin condition, even gently, is outside esthetic scope and may worsen it; refer first.
distractorExplanations.b: Recommending treatment for a medical condition amounts to diagnosing; the client should see a physician.
distractorExplanations.d: A waiver does not expand scope of practice or make it safe to treat a medical condition.

esthetician-state-readiness-check-laws-b.explanation: Referral protects the client and keeps practice legal. Avoid any unauthorized treatment.
